dietEvidence.body: The skull and dentition indicate herbivory. No gut contents are known. The long neck has been interpreted as a browsing adaptation, but the function is not demonstrated.

sizeNote: Length and mass are estimates from incomplete material, not measurements of a whole animal.
tagline: A stegosaur with an unusually long neck for its clade. The elongation is real, but its ecological significance is not established.
summary: A stegosaur with an unusually long neck for its clade. The elongation is real, but its ecological significance is not established.

discovery.body: Named by Mateus et al., 2009. The record is known from Lourinhã Formation. A partial skeleton and skull from Portugal.

fossilEvidence.title: Preserved material
fossilEvidence.body: The holotype is a partial articulated skeleton with cranial remains. A second, more complete specimen, MG 4863, was excavated in 1959 and prepared in the 2010s; it preserves anterior and posterior portions of the skeleton and is central to the validity debate.

fossilEvidence.title: Stratigraphic and geographic occurrence
fossilEvidence.body: Lourinhã Formation records the species in the Late Jurassic. The numeric range used here is ≈150–145 Ma, an occurrence estimate rather than a direct date on every specimen.

anatomy.title: Preserved anatomy
anatomy.body: The neck contains at least 17 cervical vertebrae, eight more than the ancestral ornithischian condition. Elongation involved cervicalization of anterior dorsal vertebrae and probable lengthening of the centra; the plates and tail spikes remain characteristic.

anatomy.title: Body plan
anatomy.body: The species is reconstructed as quadrupedal from the preserved limb skeleton. The posture is not observed, and the long neck's function is unresolved.

behaviour.body: Neck elongation is direct anatomy; low browsing is a hypothesis. No social or display behaviour is established.

reconstruction.body: A licensed life reconstruction is assigned to this record and credited in Sources and credits. The species is known from a partial skeleton and skull from Portugal. The reconstruction is an artist's interpretation of appearance, not a direct observation from the fossil record; preserved integument, where present, is described in the anatomy section, and the soft-tissue outline is otherwise inferred.

confidenceNote: The neck is directly preserved: at least 17 cervical vertebrae, eight more than basal ornithischians and more than most sauropods. The validity of the species is contested: Sánchez-Fenollosa et al. (2024) proposed it as a junior synonym of Dacentrurus armatus, while Costa et al. (2025) argued that MG 4863 preserves differences supporting distinction. The functional significance of the long neck is not established.
